title: The Lake Repaired Across Empires
subtitle: Seven Centuries Around a Single Lake
era: Sudarshana Lake from Mauryas to Rudradaman and Skandagupta, c. 4th century BCE-5th century CE
moral: Public works become sacred when they protect ordinary lives.

sources.citation: Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman I, Saka year 72, in D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions, vol. 1, 1965
sources.note: Primary record of the Sudarshana Lake breach, dimensions and Rudradaman's repair.

sources.citation: Junagadh inscription of Skandagupta, in D. C. Sircar, Select Inscriptions, vol. 1, 1965
sources.note: Later primary record of another repair to the same hydraulic work.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, Ancient and Early Medieval India, Pearson, 2016, pp. 48-49
sources.note: Discusses hydraulic patronage and legitimacy through the Sudarshana Lake records.

panels.shot: sweeping high-angle wide over Sudarshana Lake with Girnar hills behind and Suvishakha in the foreground

dialogue.text: At Girnar, one lake outlived Mauryas, Yavanas, Sakas and Guptas, and in its cracked stones Suvishakha, son of Kulaipa, read a seven-hundred-year duty no flood could wash away.

panels.shot: epic bird's-eye of arid Saurashtra landscape with a new reservoir gleaming

dialogue.text: Long before Rudradaman, under Chandragupta Maurya, his governor Pushyagupta dammed the streams of Girnar to form Sudarshana, a shining lake in a thirsty land.

panels.shot: medium wide on the dam with water channels extending, early morning light

dialogue.text: The inscription remembers his work: Sudarshana’s embankment, the stone raised, the waters gathered, so that fields might drink and caravans might halt by a cool shore.

panels.shot: low-angle on a Greek-looking official overseeing channels carved in stone

dialogue.text: Under Ashoka, a Yavana named Tushaspha added conduits, guiding the lake’s waters with care, proof that men from far coasts now shared in the emperor’s charge.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide, same lake across changing ages, fading empires in background

dialogue.text: Empires rose, edicts faded, new powers stamped coins in Saurashtra, yet Sudarshana held, a quiet witness, feeding villages that forgot who first ordered its stones.

panels.shot: medium close on Suvishakha reading an inscription on rock, light slanting across the script

dialogue.text: Then came the Saka year seventy-two. Under Rudradaman, his minister Suvishakha, son of Kulaipa, looked upon this old work and upon words cut into stone before his time.

panels.shot: wide shot of the lake and embankment under darkening storm clouds, Suvishakha tiny in foreground

dialogue.text: The record speaks of a violent storm. Clouds broke, winds struck, and the proud embankment faced a test harsher than any king’s decree.

panels.shot: dramatic wide of water crashing against the dam at night

dialogue.text: Rain poured, streams swelled, and Sudarshana’s calm mirror became a force. Somewhere in that dark, stones shifted and the barrier that held back life began to break.

panels.shot: morning-after wide of a breached embankment with people watching in shock

dialogue.text: By morning, the breach gaped wide. The inscription measures it in hands and cubits; the lake’s wealth now spilled uncontrolled, a blessing turned sudden peril.

panels.shot: medium on Suvishakha kneeling at the broken edge, examining with focused calm

dialogue.text: Suvishakha did not stand apart. The rock record calls him Pahlava minister, yet here he is in the broken mud, reading the breach as a scribe reads a line gone wrong.

panels.shot: intimate close-up on Suvishakha’s face as he thinks, villagers blurred behind

dialogue.speaker: suvishakha_son_of_kulaipa
dialogue.text: If this lake fails, it is not stone alone that breaks.

panels.shot: courtly interior medium shot with Suvishakha addressing unseen Rudradaman

dialogue.text: The inscription praises Rudradaman, but it is Suvishakha who is named as doer. He sought permission not to tax, not to conscript, but to repair what earlier kings had entrusted.

panels.shot: wide shot of organized workers at the dam, clearly free labourers with tools

dialogue.text: Rudradaman’s rock-edged words boast: the work was done without levying new taxes, without using forced labour. Suvishakha had to rebuild with the means already in his hands.

panels.shot: low-angle on Suvishakha guiding placement of a huge stone block

dialogue.text: Block by block, he closed the measured gap. The verse lists lengths and heights, as if to say: this is not a vague promise, but a wall of exact stone and span.

panels.shot: medium shot of Suvishakha inspecting a newly shaped spillway, water flowing gently

dialogue.text: He restored not only height but outlets, so that the next storm’s fury might find a guided path, and the lake could hold strong without drowning the land it served.

panels.shot: wide pastoral shot of full lake, irrigated fields and villagers at ease

dialogue.text: When the waters settled again behind their stone, life resumed its quieter rhythm. The same lake that once threatened now fed, the danger turned back into daily grain.

panels.shot: close shot of the Junagadh rock inscription being carved

dialogue.text: To fix this work in memory, Rudradaman’s men carved the tale on the very rock of Girnar, naming Pushyagupta, Tushaspha and Suvishakha in one flowing line of time.

panels.shot: time-shift wide showing the same rock centuries later with Skandagupta’s inscription added

dialogue.text: Yet the lake was not finished with storms. Long after Rudradaman, Skandagupta recorded another repair, another ruler answering the same call from the same worn stones.

panels.shot: concluding medium-wide of Suvishakha’s figure silhouetted against the lake and hills at sunset

dialogue.text: Sudarshana’s story shows how public works can outlast dynasties, and how a minister like Suvishakha, son of Kulaipa, makes duty to the living as enduring as any conquest cut in stone.
